![The Cheapest Ladder Is Also the Shortest](./cover.png)

Every school subject sends your parents a bill. Most of them just don't itemise
it. Chemistry wants a lab. Music wants an instrument and somebody free on
Saturday mornings to drive you to the lesson. Essays want a childhood of being
read to — a decade of unpaid tutoring dressed up as bedtime.

Maths wants a pencil.

That's the whole invoice. You can do serious mathematics on the back of a
receipt, and nobody can tell from the working whether you did it at a desk or on
a bus. Which is why maths is quietly full of broke kids.

## Nobody can argue you out of a proof

The cheapness gets all the attention. I think the bigger draw is something else:
maths tells you when you're right, and it doesn't need an adult's permission to
do it.

Picture being twelve in a house where the rules move without notice. The same
thing gets a laugh on Monday and a row on Tuesday. The grown-ups' account of
what happened last week is, let's say, creative — and you were standing right
there. Now hand that kid a proof.

The proof doesn't have moods. It isn't different today. Nobody can look them in
the eye and tell them it didn't happen that way. They can check it themselves,
at eleven at night, with no help from anyone, and simply *know* — and then keep
it somewhere nobody can get at it.

I don't think that's a small thing. I think it might be the whole thing. Maths
isn't only the subject a poor kid can afford. It's the subject that behaves,
and if not much else in your life behaves, that pull is enormous.

## The pattern turns up everywhere I've been

So the sharp, broke kids go into maths. I grew up poor in London, and I've since
spent time in Mexico City, Guadalajara, Guatemala City, Bogotá and Manila. Same
story in all six. Different languages, same kid at the back working three
chapters ahead of everyone, because the problems are the one thing that's
reliably there.

That's six cities and a lifetime of anecdote, not a dataset. I have no numbers,
and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claimed to.

Here's what nobody mentioned to any of us: the ladder is shorter than it looks.

## The bill arrives at twenty-two

Entry costs a pencil. Exit costs about a decade.

You get recruited on the first price, which is honest, advertised and roughly
zero. The second price — years of low pay after school, plus the network you'd
need to turn all those credentials into actual money — never comes up. Partly
because the people best placed to quote it are the ones who never had to pay it.

And the destinations are fine! Teaching, statistics, actuarial work: real jobs,
stable, respectable, the kind that make your family proud of you at weddings.
They also sit well below where the same brain lands with a family behind it.
Nobody lied. The subject kept every promise it made. It just made fewer promises
than you thought it had.

## There's a way off the ladder, and it's a browser tab

Now the good news, and I do think this is good news.

Every browser on earth has a JavaScript console sitting inside it. Right-click,
Inspect, and you're in. No licence, no install, no permission, no adult, no
money. A sharp fifteen-year-old who ended up doing maths because maths was the
affordable option can be running real code within the minute — and computational
work pays what pure maths does not.

It's the same trick maths pulled, when you look at it. Cheap. Checkable without
asking anybody. You type the thing, it works or it doesn't, and the machine has
no opinion about who your parents are.

I find that genuinely cheering. Then I think about what it actually needs, and
I stop finding it cheering.

## But it charges rent on the room

Not the machine. Or not only the machine, which is the part everyone fixates on.

It needs a desk, or something you can pretend is a desk. A chair. A socket that
works and power that stays on. A couple of hours where nobody else wants the
table for dinner, ironing, homework or a card game. And quiet — not silence,
just enough calm to keep a half-finished idea alive in your head while somebody
walks through the room. When you're learning to build things, a half-finished
idea is the only kind you ever have.

A phone won't cover it. I know everyone has a phone. You cannot sit at a phone
for three hours, and everything that makes it good on the bus makes it hopeless
for building.

A pencil asks for none of this, and that is the entire point of a pencil. It
works on the floor. It works on the bus. It works in ten-minute pieces stolen
between other people's demands on you. Of everything in this essay, it's the
only tool that doesn't care what room it's in.

Which is the part that gets me. The kid this whole essay is about — the one who
fell for maths because home didn't hold still — is exactly the kid without the
quiet corner and the free evening. The thing that pulled them into maths is the
same thing that keeps them there.

So the new ladder pays better than the old one and is harder to get onto. Worse,
the sorting has moved somewhere nobody's watching. Not admissions. Not the
scholarship. Not the exam. Years earlier than any of those, in whether the house
had a corner that was yours for two hours and a socket that worked. I don't know
how you'd fund that. I'm not sure many funders know it's the thing to fund.

Maths was cheap because it never asked about the room you were standing in. The
new one asks for the room.
